Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette: Liam's conviction that the world remained a hostile place-shaped by the night his refugee journey was cut short by a sudden, violent raid-fueled an ever-present state of alert. Because he believed danger lurked in every corner, he began to steer clear of any conversation that might stir memories, silently avoiding colleagues who asked about his past. He started checking his thoughts for signs of mental breakdown, an internal vigil that replaced normal reflection. His persistent sense of peril also colored the way his mind stored the ordeal. Rather than recalling the event as a fluid narrative, Liam's mind froze moments as stark images, his body's trembling position replaying with each recollection. The absence of a coherent story left him feeling as if he were still in that cramped, overcrowded shelter, his emotions erupting whenever the memory surfaced without a clear visual cue. When those fragmented images rose from the depths of his mind, the sounds of a city-car horns, distant sirens, even the quiet hum of a building-triggered his startle reflex, jolting him as if a threat had materialized. The sudden noises would make his chest tighten, and in the silence that followed he sensed a danger waiting to strike. Even ordinary sounds seemed to loom with menace, and the sudden realization of being in "danger" felt almost automatic. Each recall of the harrowing night reinforced Liam's belief that the world was unsafe. The vivid visual and bodily cues served as constant reminders that his past had not ended; instead, it had woven itself into his present perception of reality. This deepening conviction made the memory a living, breathing entity that kept his sense of danger alive. The persistent threats in his mind pushed Liam toward avoidance and hyper-monitoring. In courtrooms where the air was thick with the scent of coffee and the low murmur of attorneys, he found himself preemptively checking the room for any sound that might unbalance him. He refused to discuss his past with his partner or coworkers, fearing that sharing could trigger the same startle response or cause him to lose his composure in front of clients. These heightened threat reactions also sharpened the vividness of his memories. Each time a new alarm or sudden silence occurred, he would be flooded with a flash of that night's terror-his hands trembling, the weight of a gun felt in his chest. The cycle of threat and memory made each recall feel immediate and unmediated, blurring the boundary between past and present. The continual sense of danger also amplified Liam's hypervigilance, feeding into his core belief that the world was perilous. He felt compelled to scan every hallway for unseen threats, to pause before stepping through doors, to stay awake even when he was exhausted. This hyper-awareness kept his senses on high alert, leaving him exhausted and emotionally drained, and reinforcing his conviction that danger lurked around every corner. Because Liam's avoidance, constant thought monitoring, and refusal to engage in conversation kept the threat vivid, his negative appraisal of the world remained unchallenged. The more he stayed away from triggers, the more the world seemed hostile, and the deeper the belief that his mind would unravel at any moment. Now, after weeks of sleepless nights and a case loss that made him doubt his competence, he has finally reached out for help, hoping to break this relentless loop and reclaim a sense of safety.
